metadata.name: Chronic constipation
metadata.emergency_level: Routine - but red flags (bleeding, weight loss, new onset >50) need investigation; faecal impaction/obstruction can be urgent
metadata.severity: Common and usually benign; can cause significant discomfort and complications

overview.short_description: Persistently infrequent, difficult, or incomplete defecation (hard stools, straining) for at least several months, usually functional and managed with lifestyle measures and laxatives.
overview.detailed_description: Chronic constipation is very common, especially in women, the elderly and those on certain drugs. Most is functional/primary. Management is a stepped approach: lifestyle (fibre, fluids, activity, toileting), then laxatives (bulk-forming, then osmotic/stimulant, then newer agents). The main safety task is to identify red flags suggesting colorectal cancer or obstruction and to recognise and treat faecal impaction.
overview.pathophysiology: Reduced colonic motility (slow transit), disordered defecation (pelvic floor dyssynergia), and/or a normal-transit functional disorder produce hard, infrequent or difficult-to-pass stool; low fibre/fluid and inactivity contribute.
overview.etiology: Primary/functional (most). Secondary: drugs (opioids, iron, anticholinergics, calcium-channel blockers, some antidepressants), metabolic/endocrine (hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, diabetes), neurological (Parkinson's, spinal disease), obstruction (stricture, cancer), painful anorectal conditions, and reduced mobility/dehydration.
overview.natural_history: Often chronic/relapsing; responds to lifestyle and laxatives in most.
overview.prognosis: Good; the concern is missing an underlying secondary cause (especially colorectal cancer).

prevalence.value: Very common; affects a substantial proportion of adults, more with age and in women.

incidence.value: High; increases with age, immobility and medication use.

mortality.value: Very low directly; relevant via complications or an underlying cause.

epidemiology.age_groups: All ages; commoner in the elderly.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Low-fibre diet, low fluid intake, physical inactivity, ignoring the urge to defecate.
risk_factors.medications: Opioids (very common cause), iron, anticholinergics, calcium-channel blockers, some antidepressants/antipsychotics, antacids (aluminium/calcium).
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, Parkinson's, spinal cord disease, anorectal disease, prior obstruction.

symptoms.symptom: Sensation of incomplete evacuation / anorectal blockage

symptoms.importance: Suggests faecal impaction (do not treat as simple diarrhoea)

symptoms.symptom: Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or new onset >50 (RED FLAGS)
symptoms.importance: RED FLAGS - investigate for colorectal cancer/obstruction

negative_findings.finding: No rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, abdominal/rectal mass, or new change >50
negative_findings.why_important: Absence of red flags supports benign functional constipation

negative_findings.finding: No features of obstruction (severe pain, distension, vomiting, no flatus)

history_questions.question: How often do you open your bowels, and are stools hard with straining or incomplete emptying?
history_questions.why_ask: Defines constipation and possible defecatory disorder

history_questions.question: Any rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a recent change in bowel habit (especially over 50)?
What medications do you take (especially opioids, iron)?
Any symptoms of hypothyroidism, or neurological disease?
Any severe pain, distension, vomiting, or not passing wind (obstruction)?

physical_examination.expected_finding: May feel loaded colon; a mass or distension is a red flag
Hard stool/impaction; assess for mass, and anorectal disease; pelvic floor function

physical_examination.examination: Signs of a secondary cause (thyroid, neurological)

vital_signs.bmi: Variable (weight loss is a red flag)

laboratory_tests.indication: If a secondary cause is suspected or red flags present

laboratory_tests.test_name: Faecal immunochemical test (FIT) / referral per cancer pathway
laboratory_tests.indication: Red flags or change in bowel habit

other_diagnostic_tests.endoscopy: Colonoscopy for red flags / to exclude organic disease
other_diagnostic_tests.biopsy: As part of colonoscopy if indicated
other_diagnostic_tests.anorectal_physiology: Anorectal manometry/defecography for suspected defecatory disorder (specialist)

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical (Rome IV functional constipation): >=2 of straining, hard/lumpy stools, sensation of incomplete evacuation, sensation of anorectal obstruction, manual manoeuvres, and <3 spontaneous bowel movements/week - for the last 3 months (onset >=6 months). Exclude red flags and secondary causes.
diagnostic_criteria.diagnostic_scores: Bristol stool chart; Rome IV criteria.

differential_diagnosis.differences: Bleeding, weight loss, older, mass, progressive
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any bleeding, weight loss, or new change over 50?
Do you take opioids/iron, or have thyroid/neurological disease?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Excessive straining, digitation, incomplete emptying with normal transit
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Do you strain a lot or need to press to empty despite the urge?
Do you have leakage/soiling with a blocked feeling?

diagnostic_questions.question: Any rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a new persistent change in bowel habit (especially over 50)?
Do you take opioids or iron, or have thyroid/neurological disease?

next_best_question.question: Any red flags, what medications, and is there overflow soiling or straining/incomplete emptying?
next_best_question.expected_answers: Red flags / secondary cause / defecatory disorder
next_best_question.branching_logic: Red flags -> investigate; secondary -> treat cause; functional -> lifestyle + stepped laxatives; impaction -> disimpaction regimen; defecatory disorder -> pelvic floor therapy

next_best_test.why: Detect impaction, mass, and defecatory dysfunction

next_best_test.test: Bloods/FIT/colonoscopy (if red flags or secondary cause suspected)

red_flags.finding: Rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss, abdominal/rectal mass, or new change in bowel habit over 50
Features of obstruction (severe pain, distension, vomiting, no flatus)

red_flags.immediate_action: Disimpaction regimen; do not treat as simple diarrhoea

red_flags.finding: New neurological symptoms (e.g., cauda equina features with constipation/retention)

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Red flags for colorectal cancer; obstruction; cauda equina.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Refractory constipation, suspected defecatory disorder (pelvic floor), or diagnostic uncertainty.
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Bowel obstruction or cauda equina syndrome.

initial_management.supportive_care: Explain and reassure (usually benign); optimise toileting habits (respond to urge, correct posture, unhurried time).
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Soluble fibre/bulk-forming agent; Polyethylene glycol/macrogol; Stimulant laxative; Prescription secretagogue/prucalopride/PAMORA. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: AGA_ACG_CIC_2023.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Increase dietary fibre gradually, adequate fluids, regular physical activity, and good toileting routine; review causative drugs.
initial_management.follow_up: Review response; titrate/step laxatives; investigate if not improving or red flags develop.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Stepped laxatives: bulk-forming (with adequate fluids) first for most; add/switch to an osmotic (e.g., macrogol) then a stimulant (e.g., senna/bisacodyl); newer agents (e.g., prucalopride, linaclotide) for refractory cases per criteria. Use a specific opioid-induced constipation approach (osmotic/stimulant +/- PAMORA) for opioid users. Disimpaction regimen for faecal impaction.

patient_education.home_advice: Constipation is very common and usually not serious. Eating more fibre, drinking enough fluids, staying active, and not putting off going to the toilet all help. If needed, laxatives are safe and effective - start with a fibre or osmotic type. See a doctor if you see blood, lose weight, or your bowel habit changes and stays changed (especially over 50), or if you have severe pain, a swollen tummy and vomiting.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: الإمساك شائع جداً وغالباً غير خطير. يفيد تناول مزيد من الألياف، وشرب سوائل كافية، والحفاظ على النشاط، وعدم تأجيل الذهاب للحمّام. وعند الحاجة، المُليّنات آمنة وفعّالة - ابدأ بنوع ليفي أو تناضحي. راجع الطبيب إذا رأيت دماً، أو نقص وزنك، أو تغيّرت عادة الأمعاء واستمرّ التغيّر (خاصةً فوق الخمسين)، أو حدث ألم شديد وانتفاخ بطن وقيء.
patient_education.prevention: Fibre, fluids, activity, good toileting habits; anticipate and prevent opioid-induced constipation.
patient_education.warning_signs: Rectal bleeding, weight loss, persistent change in bowel habit, severe pain with distension/vomiting, or overflow soiling.

prevention.lifestyle: Fibre, fluids, activity, toileting habits; laxatives when starting opioids.

evidence.evidence_level: High for laxatives; moderate for lifestyle measures.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by AGA_ACG_CIC_2023; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
evidence.legacy_guideline_strength_pre_v13: Strong - NICE CKS, Rome IV, specialist society guidance.
